transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17
Start time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Torres (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (Redwood CSM); Mark Rivera (Foxglove Lead ML Eng), Sana Iqbal (Platform), Tom O'Neill (CTO), Ava (Data Scientist)
Recording id: ff-20261117-foxglove-01

Summary:
Quick run-through of pilot metrics from last week: KV hit rate dipped during midday surge, prefix reuse patterns causing cold misses, discussed tunables (TTL, prefix coalescing, session affinity), agreed on bench plan and data handoff. Action items assigned.

Topics:
- KV / prefix hit-rate trends
- Prompt reuse strategy and signature normalization
- Eviction policy and TTL tradeoffs
- Synthetic bench plan and next steps for rollouts
- Security/ops: SSO and KMS questions surfaced

Notes on artifacts shared:
- Redwood: pilot-dashboard.csv (link shared in chat), eviction-policy-proposal.pdf (link), bench-config.yaml (Gist link)
- Foxglove: sample_anon_traffic.tar.gz (to be shared via S3)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jamie (AE): Okay, hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll start — this is the weekly sync for the Foxglove prefetch pilot. We've got about 40 minutes. Priya is going to walk through the numbers and then we'll triage the midday surge that Mark mentioned.

[00:18] Priya (SE): Thanks Jamie. Uh, quick TL;DR, overall KV hit rate improved from 42% to 57% after the initial prefix coalescing we pushed last week, but there's a noticeable drop to ~28% during 11:30 to 13:30 local time which corresponds to the surge. I pulled the chart into the dashboard, link in chat — apologies, the export labels are messy, some of the model names got truncated.

[00:44] Mark (Foxglove): Yeah that midday dip is the problem. Our users run bulk analysis jobs then, and the traffic is more varied. Also we noticed more unique prefixes because of dynamic user IDs baked into prompts.

[01:06] Sana (Platform): to add, our templating injects session ids sometimes, so prefixes that look identical to humans appear different to the cache key. We've been trying a regex strip at the app layer but it breaks when the user intentionally includes a number, so we flipped the toggle off.

[01:30] Priya: Right, so two levers — app-side normalization (good for client-owned changes) and server-side canonicalization where we canonicalize known token patterns before computing the KV key. Server-side helps when you can't change hundreds of microservices. Drawbacks are potential false merges if canonicalization is too permissive.

[01:54] Tom (CTO): Quick question — can Redwood's server-side canonicalization be made opt-in per route? We have some prompts where numbers are semantically important.

[02:06] Priya: Yes, per-route canonicalizers are supported. You configure a small Python-ish transform or a regex set, and it runs in the pre-hash phase. We ship a few templates, but we can accept custom logic — within sandboxed rules for safety. There can be a small exec cost but it's microseconds.

[02:30] Ava (Data Sci): I'm worried about over-normalizing. For our summarization, a user id can change tone; merging could reduce personalization. How do we measure if merging hurts quality?

[02:42] Priya: Great point. We recommend a guardrail: keep a sample of merged vs non-merged requests and compare ROUGE/BLEU or qualitative checks. Also maintain a fallback to bypass cache for routes flagged as sensitive. We can run A/B with canary rates.

[03:10] Mark: On the eviction policy you recommended TTL 1hr initially, then we tried 30m; during the surge that still caused thrashing. Can you explain the prefix coalescing TTL interplay?

[03:28] Priya: Sure. Prefix coalescing groups similar prefixes into a canonical bucket to share KV entries. If TTL is too short relative to user revisit patterns, you get churn. On the other hand, very long TTL raises stale result risk for dynamic prompts. With your traffic we saw median revisit at ~22 minutes, 90th at 2 hours. So a TTL of 15-30 minutes with a small LRU margin plus occasional background re-materialization might be best for cost/latency balance.

[04:05] Jamie: I pulled up the CSV — there's a column 'pref_hh' that is basically the prefix hash grouping, but some groups are massive and some are singletons — the long tail is killing the mid-day numbers.

[04:25] Mark: Those singletons are mainly prompts including timestamps and filenames. We can try to normalize filenames out, but it's a lot of engineers.

[04:40] Priya: We proposed two mitigation experiments: 1) server-side mild canonicalization for known noisy token types + TTL 15m; 2) prefix coalescing threshold adjustment — increase the coalesce threshold so extremely rare prefixes don't create their own buckets but instead fall back to a parent bucket. That reduces cold misses but may increase slight reduction in quality.

[05:08] Sana: How do we pick the parent bucket? Is it semantic? We can't just hash to the first N tokens because of data leakage concerns.

[05:20] Priya: It's rule-based: you pick a token-suppression policy (numbers, filepaths, emails) and a similarity function that respects token positions. We also keep a telemetry flag so you can see which canonicalizations fired.

[05:38] Tom: Is there an audit trail? We need to show if canonicalization changed inputs for GDPR audit.

[05:46] Priya: Yes, we log canonicalizer applied, original and canonicalized snippet hashes (not full text by default) and a pointer to masked payload if requested. We can redact PII on export. That satisfies SOC2/ISO auditors — of course we will share docs.

[06:08] Mark: Okay, good. On the bench results you ran last night — can you walk through cost vs latency?

[06:18] Priya: The synthetic bench used a 10k request set with your prefix distribution. With prefix coalescing + TTL30m we saw average p99 latency drop from 820ms to 510ms and token cost per 1k tokens decreased ~22%. But during a 5k simultaneous burst the KV hit rate dropped to 31% and p99 spiked to ~1.2s. That was the midday pattern replicated.

[06:48] Jamie: The big takeaway is burst-capacity and the ability to warm the KV layer before bursts. We suggested two operational mitigations: pre-warm (scheduled background warm-ups for top prefixes) and session affinity to route burst traffic to warmed instances.

[07:10] Mark: Pre-warm sounds good, but can we do it without duplicating user data? We need to keep PII out.

[07:18] Priya: Pre-warm uses synthetic canonicalized inputs derived from the prefix list — we don't store raw user text; we generate anonymized facsimiles. The pre-warm process is rate-limited and respects retention rules.

[07:33] Ava: For pre-warm, if you warm with an anonymized prompt, will the model output be representative so that cache hits are valid for real traffic?

[07:44] Priya: Usually yes for prefix-level reuse where the prefix determines the first few tokens; but if the suffix changes the output semantics significantly then you need a longer context warm. We can warm with multiple suffix variants to increase coverage.

[08:04] Mark: Okay, what about session affinity? That seems trickier for our distributed users.

[08:12] Priya: Session affinity maps similar session keys to the same inference pool so the KV cache residency increases. For stateless clients it's a header-based affinity or a signed cookie. Tradeoffs: it reduces global utilization smoothing but increases per-session cache hit rates. Works best when traffic is skewed by user.

[08:36] Sana: Passing cookies through our mobile clients is doable but requires SDK bump. Might be a small roll.

[08:46] Tom: If we do affinity plus pre-warm, do we still need Dedicated? We're evaluating Dedicated for predictable latency.

[08:56] Jamie: Dedicated helps with predictable throughput and reserved burst capacity. For cost, Hosted with smart routing and pre-warm can get you most of the benefits, but Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and you can control eviction granularly. We'll send a delta pricing table.

[09:12] Mark: Competitors — BigCloudAI claims a 'persistent KV' feature, is that comparable?

[09:20] Priya: I think their persistent KV is stronger for pure key-value stores, but our runtime integrates KV with KV-cache aware execution and prefix-aware coalescing. The integration means fewer duplicate model runs for partial-key matches. But we can do a side-by-side bench if you want.

[09:40] Ava: On measurement — what's our success metric for this pilot? Hit rate target? p99? cost delta?

[09:48] Jamie: We suggested pilot success = p99 latency <= 600ms for 95% of 24h windows and average KV hit rate >= 60% during top-traffic windows, plus <= 15% token-cost delta vs baseline. Those are negotiable.

[10:10] Mark: I think p99 600ms is good. We'll sign off on 60% hit-rate target as long as quality regressions are under 2% measured by our eval set.

[10:24] Priya: We'll instrument a quality gate — we'll keep an eval set of 500 prompts and monitor top-line similarity and flag regressions. If regression > 2% we'll auto-disable the canonicalizer for that route.

[10:42] Jamie: Quick ops question from Liam — do we have a recommended alert threshold?

[10:48] Liam (CSM): Yeah, we usually alert if KV hit rate drops >20% vs baseline for 10 minutes or p99 >800ms for 5 minutes. We can set that up in the Console and ship an alert webhook to your PagerDuty.

[11:05] Mark: perfect. On the data side, we'll share the anonymized S3 bucket by Friday. Expect some cleanup by our infra folks.

[11:14] Tom: On security — can Redwood integrate with our KMS? We want keys managed within our cloud.

[11:20] Jamie: Yes — Private and Dedicated support external KMS/HSM integrations. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys via KMS. We'll share the security brief and SOC2 artifacts.

[11:32] Sana: Also SSO — we need SAML for console access and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.

[11:38] Jamie: SAML SSO and audit log forwarding are standard for enterprise tiers. We'll include config steps in the doc jam.

[11:46] Priya: Back to technical tunables — another small win is adaptive eviction: when we detect a sustained surge we increase eviction threshold for low-frequency prefixes so hot buckets remain. This requires a short warm-up job post-surge, but it curbs thrash. We can prototype that in the bench.

[12:10] Mark: Sounds promising. Can you model cost implications?

[12:15] Priya: We have a model that estimates token-cost per 1M requests given hit rate and model size. For your distribution, moving from 32% to 60% hit rate reduces inference token units by roughly 30% — but pre-warm adds some overhead (~2-4% extra). Net should still be positive. We'll share the spreadsheet.

[12:36] Ava: Do we have telemetry for prefix-level quality degradation? I want to see per-prefix delta.

[12:42] Priya: Yes — Console exposes per-prefix buckets with hit rate, avg latency, and a 'quality delta' metric if you upload the eval set mapping. We can onboard that for you.

[12:56] Mark: Alright so concrete plan: Redwood runs the 50k synthetic bench with adaptive eviction + TTL15m + coalesce threshold tweak, we compare results and then we schedule a deep-dive with our infra to talk session affinity.

[13:14] Jamie: Correct. Also Jamie to send pricing delta and the security docs.

[13:20] Tom: One last thing — can we get a short runbook if the KV layer is misbehaving? We need steps to triage in production.

[13:28] Liam: We'll draft a runbook excerpt: how to toggle canonicalizers, increase TTL, failover to smaller model, and emergency eviction steps. I'll put that on the action items.

[13:43] Priya: I'll start the bench tonight and will post results in the channel. Expect raw CSV and a summary. The bench will simulate the midday surge.

[13:52] Mark: Great. Thanks everyone.

[13:57] Jamie: Recap of next steps in chat: Redwood bench + CSV, Foxglove share traffic, schedule infra deep-dive next week. Anything else?

[14:08] Tom: No, that's it. Thanks.

[14:12] Jamie: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.

[14:20] (meeting ended)
